label: 1v
quote: Wahrscheinlich führt diese Frage auf die Lie'sche Theo- rie der [-Funktionen-] [-gruppen-] gruppen.
english: Probably this question leads to Lie's theory of groups.
topic: The page derives a mean cohesive force from shifted electron distances, poses a Hamilton–Jacobi question about characterizing two-parameter families of solutions of intermediate first-order differential equations belonging to a given field, and notes the eigenvalue behaviour of the Hermite-type equation $y''-2xy'+2ny=0$.

triage.modern_statement: My best reading, which I could not confirm: given a field of extremals for a variational problem or a second-order ODE, Hilbert asks for a description of the two-parameter families of solutions of intermediate first-order integrals that belong to that field. In Hamilton–Jacobi terms, this means describing the complete integrals z=f(x,y;a,b) of the associated first-order PDE, with the condition ∂(z,p)/∂(a,b)≠0, that are compatible with the field. His conjecture is that this classification belongs to Lie's theory of transformation groups, presumably including contact transformations and integration methods for first-order PDEs. The note gives no exact equation, hypotheses or claim that can be checked, so it cannot be stated as a precise theorem.
triage.answered_by: No later source answers this specific note. The general area — complete integrals, Hamilton–Jacobi/Jacobi theory of first-order PDEs, Lie's contact transformations and the integration of complete systems, and Hilbert's invariant integral for fields of extremals — was classical and well developed by Jacobi, Lie, Weierstrass/Hilbert and others, but I found no work that specifically settles this conjecture.

evidence.claim: A complete integral is a family of solutions of a first-order PDE that depends on two parameters (a,b) and satisfies a Jacobian non-degeneracy condition. This matches the 'two-parameter families of solutions' in the note.
Lie studied contact transformations and continuous transformation groups in connection with differential equations. This links the subject to the 'Lie theory of groups' that Hilbert expected.
Lie gave a new interpretation of solutions to complete systems and tried to find all systems of differential equations that admit a given group of infinitesimal transformations.
Lie built on Jacobi's theory of first-order PDEs, including Lie's construction of complete equations.
Hilbert's invariant integral connects fields of extremals with a system of first-order PDEs (the Hamilton–Jacobi setting). This is the standard framework for solutions that 'belong to a given field'.

triage.why: The note is a one-line guess that a vaguely stated Hamilton–Jacobi question will 'probably' lead to Lie's group theory. It has no precise statement that could be proved or disproved. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. It is only loosely related to Problem 23 (calculus of variations). The links between complete integrals, fields of extremals and Lie's contact-transformation/group methods for first-order PDEs were classical by Hilbert's time. However, I found no source that takes up this particular conjecture. I did only a few web searches and did not try to date the page. I cannot say whether the specific question was ever answered.
